(p-٥٧٨٠) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surah As-Saff

It is also called Surat al-Hawariyyin (the Surah of the Disciples). It is Medinan. There is no weight to the view that it is Meccan, because its verses that urge fighting (al-qital) refute it, since jihad was not prescribed except in Medina. Its number of verses is fourteen.

(p-٥٧٨١) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Discourse on the interpretation (ta'wil) of His saying, Exalted is He:

[1] ﴿Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth glorifies Allah, and He is the Exalted in Might, the Wise.﴾

﴿Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth glorifies Allah, and He is the Exalted in Might, the Wise.﴾ That is: every creature of His, the higher and the lower, submitted to Allah and yielded to His subjugation, and it points to His divinity (uluhiyyah) and His lordship (rububiyyah). Its explanation has already preceded.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[2–3] ﴿O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do?﴾ ﴿It is greatly hateful in the sight of Allah that you say what you do not do.﴾ [al-Saff: 3]

﴿Why do you say what you do not do?﴾ Al-Qashani said: Among the necessary consequences of true faith are truthfulness and steadfastness of resolve, since the purity of the innate nature (fitrah), free from the defects of upbringing, requires both of them. His words, ﴿It is greatly hateful in the sight of Allah that you say what you do not do﴾ [al-Saff: 3], may include lying and breaking a promise. Whoever claims faith is obliged, by the ruling of faith, to avoid both of them; otherwise there is no reality to his faith. Therefore He said: "what you do not do," because lying contradicts manliness (muruwwah), which is among the foundations of faith, let alone its perfection. For original faith is a return to the primordial nature (al-fitrah al-ula) and the upright religion (al-din al-qayyim), and this entails all kinds of virtues in all their varieties, the lowest degree of which is chastity (iffah), which requires manliness. The liar has no manliness, so he has no real faith. We say he has no manliness because speech is informative utterance that conveys meaning to another, indicated by the word. The distinctive characteristic that distinguishes man from others is speech. When the report does not correspond to reality, the benefit of speech is not achieved, and so its speaker leaves humanity; he has conveyed what does not correspond to reality, namely the belief that what did not occur has occurred, and so he enters the definition of satanic conduct (al-shaytanah), and thus deserves great hatred in the sight of Allah, by squandering his capacity and acquiring what contradicts it, its opposites. The same applies to breaking a promise, because it is close to lying, and because sincerity and steadfastness of resolve are necessary consequences of courage, which is one of the virtues necessary for soundness of nature and its first degree. When these are absent, original faith is absent, since its necessary consequence is absent, and so hatred from Allah is established. End of quotation.

A subtle point:

Al-Zamakhshari said: This is among the most eloquent and expressive speech in its meaning. In (kabura) he intended amazement, expressed without its own verb. The meaning of amazement is magnifying the matter in the hearts of the listeners. He attributed (kabura) to (an taqulu), and put (maqtan) in the accusative as its specification, indicating that their saying what they do not do is pure hatred with no admixture, due to the intense firmness of hatred in it. The word (al-maqt) was chosen because it is the most intense and most forceful hatred. He did not limit himself to making the hatred great, but made it the most severe and most grievous. And (ʿinda Allah) is more forceful than that, because once the greatness of His hatred is established in the sight of Allah, its greatness and intensity are complete.

Al-Nasir said: Beyond these four aspects there is a fifth aspect, which is the repetition of His words ﴿what you do not do﴾, a single phrase within a single utterance. Among the benefits of repetition is awe-inspiring emphasis and magnification.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[2–3] ﴿O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do?﴾ ﴿It is greatly hateful in the sight of Allah that you say what you do not do.﴾ [al-Saff: 3]

**The interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:**

[4] ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who fight in His cause in ranks, as if they were a solid structure.﴾

﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who fight in His cause in ranks, as if they were a solid structure.﴾ Al-Qashani said: "Because giving up the self in the cause of Allah occurs only when the self is purely devoted to love of Allah, for a person loves everything other than Allah only for his own self. So the root of polytheism and of loving rivals is self-love. When he gives up the self, he is not loving his own self. And when he does not love his self, he necessarily does not love any worldly thing. When his expenditure of himself is for the sake of Allah and His cause, and not for the sake of the self, as he said, 'He left the world for the world,' [p. 5783] the love of Allah in his heart outweighs the love of everything else. He is then among those of whom He said: ﴿But those who believe are stronger in love for Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 165]. And when they are like this, Allah's love for them necessarily follows, because of His words: ﴿He loves them and they love Him﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 54]." End of quotation.

**Remarks:**

**The first:** The mention of this verse right after the condemnation of those who stay behind is evidence that the condemnation was connected to the words of those who were promised steadfastness in fighting the disbelievers, and then did not keep their word. End of quotation.

Al-Nasir supported this from the standpoint of rhetoric, saying that the first (general prohibition) serves as a general introduction to this particular story, like His words: ﴿O you who believe, do not put yourselves forward before Allah and His Messenger, and fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is Hearing and Knowing﴾ [al-Hujurat: 1], and ﴿O you who believe, do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet﴾ [al-Hujurat: 2]. So the general prohibition came first, and the intended meaning is that this particular case is included within it, just as you say to someone who has committed a specific offence: "Do not do what brings shame upon you, and do not insult Zayd." The benefit of such a construction is prohibiting one thing twice, once as included within the general and once singled out specifically. This is preferable to prohibiting it twice in particular, since that would be counted as repetition, whereas this includes a repetition together with the magnification and emphasis contained in generalization. End of quotation.

**The second:** In al-Iklil, al-Kiya al-Harrasi said: One may argue from His words ﴿Why do you say what you do not do?﴾ [al-Saff: 2] and ﴿It is greatly hateful in the sight of Allah that you say what you do not do﴾ [al-Saff: 3] for the obligation to fulfil vows (nadhr) and the vow of obstinacy (nadhr al-lajaj), and others added: and promises. End of quotation.

Ibn Kathir said: This is a rebuke of one who makes a promise or says a statement and does not keep it. For this reason, some of the scholars of the early generations (al-salaf) used this noble verse as evidence that it is obligatory to keep a promise unconditionally, whether or not the one promised has acted upon it. They also argued from the Sunnah, what is established in the two Sahih collections, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The sign of the hypocrite is three: when he promises he breaks it, when he speaks he lies, and when he is entrusted he betrays." For this reason Allah, may He be exalted, emphasised this rebuke against them with His words: ﴿It is greatly hateful in the sight of Allah that you say what you do not do﴾ [al-Saff: 3].

Imam Ahmad and Abu Dawud related from Abdullah ibn Amir ibn Rabi'ah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ came to us while I was a child. I went out to play, and my mother said: 'Abdullah! Come, I will give you something.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'And what did you intend to give him?' She said: 'Dates.' He said: 'As for you, if you had not done so, a lie would have been written against you.'"

Imam Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, held that if a promise is linked to a resolve on the part of the one promised, it becomes obligatory to fulfil it, as when someone says to another: "Marry, and I will give you such-and-such every day." So he married, and it became obligatory upon him to give it for as long as this continued, because the right of a human being is attached to it.

The majority held that it is not obligatory in any case. They interpreted the verse as having been revealed when they wished that the obligation of jihad would be prescribed for them, and when it was prescribed some of them shrank from it, like His words: ﴿Have you not seen those to whom it was said, "Restrain your hands and establish prayer and give zakah"? But when fighting was prescribed for them, behold, a party of them feared men as they would fear Allah or with greater fear, and said, "Our Lord, why have You prescribed fighting for us? If only You had delayed us for a short time." Say: "The enjoyment of this world is little, and the Hereafter is better for one who fears Allah, and you will not be wronged, [even as much as] a thread."﴾ [al-Nisa': 77]. And He said: ﴿Those who believe say, "If only a surah were sent down." But when a decisive surah was sent down and fighting was mentioned therein, you saw those in whose hearts is disease looking at you with the look of one fainting in the throes of death﴾ [Muhammad: 20], to the end of the verse. Likewise, the meaning of this verse is as Ibn Abbas said: "Some of the believers, before jihad was prescribed, used to say: 'We wish Allah, mighty and majestic, would show us the most beloved of deeds to Him, so that we might act upon it.' So Allah informed His Prophet that the most beloved of deeds to Him is faith in Him without doubt, and striving against the people of His disobedience who opposed faith and did not acknowledge it. When fighting was prescribed, some of the believers disliked it, and its command weighed heavily upon them, so Allah sent down: ﴿O you who believe, why do you say what you do not do?﴾ [al-Saff: 2]." It was also said: The Muslims used to say: "If we knew which deeds are most beloved to Allah, we would undertake them, even if our souls and wealth were lost in them." Then, on the day of Uhud, they turned away from the Prophet ﷺ, until he was wounded in the head and his front tooth was broken, and Allah sent down: ﴿O you who believe, why do you say what you do not do?﴾ [al-Saff: 2]. This was related from Muqatil ibn Hayyan.

It was also said: This was revealed as a rebuke to a group of hypocrites who used to promise the believers victory while they were lying. They would say: "If you go out, we will go out with you, and we will be in your support, and in... and in......" This was related from Ibn Zayd.

All of what has been related here is included within the verse.

Imam Ahmad related from Abdullah ibn Salam, who said: "We discussed among ourselves which of us would come to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and ask him: 'Which deeds are most beloved to Allah?' None of us stood up. So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent for us a man who gathered us, and he recited to us this surah, meaning the Surah al-Saff, in its entirety." The wording of Ibn Abi Hatim from Abdullah ibn Salam is: "Some of the companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'If we sent someone to the Messenger of Allah to ask him about that.' He said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ called those men one by one until he had gathered them, and this surah, al-Saff, was revealed concerning them. Abdullah ibn Salam said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited it to us in its entirety."

In the narration of Ibn Abi Hatim there is a great benefit: namely, that the companion's statement "this surah was revealed" means it was recited in connection with the incident, as the narration before it makes clear. Narrations explain one another. We have pointed this out repeatedly.

**The third:** In al-Iklil, concerning His words ﴿as if they were a solid structure﴾: it indicates the desirability of the fighters standing in rows in battle, like the rows in prayer, and that it is desirable to close gaps and fill the lacks in the rows, to complete the first row before the next, and to make the rows straight, foot to foot, so that none of them advances ahead of another. End of quotation.

Ibn Abi al-Faras said: It has also been used as evidence that the fighting of infantry is superior to the fighting of cavalry, because close-packed formation is only possible for them. He said: This is disputed. End of quotation.

There are two other interpretations of the simile:

The first: that what is meant is steadfastness and the firmness of feet in the position, as a warning that one whose feet are unsteady and who wavers in his position is far from those whom Allah, may He be exalted, hates, and does not attain His love, let alone one who resolves to flee.

The second: that what is meant is the unity of word and agreement on a unified stand against the enemy, so that they are united and mutually supportive like a solid structure. Al-Razi alluded to these two interpretations. These two are closer than the first, because they strengthen the meaning of the opening of the surah, concerning steadfastness in keeping and fulfilling a promise, and the rebuke of one who breaks it, as has preceded.

The Discourse on the Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[5] ﴿And when Moses said to his people, "O my people, why do you harm me, while you know that I am the Messenger of God to you?" So when they deviated, God caused their hearts to deviate. And God does not guide the defiantly disobedient people.﴾

﴿And when Moses said to his people, "O my people, why do you harm me, while you know that I am the Messenger of God to you"﴾ That is: why do you inflict harm upon me by opposing and disobeying what I command you, while you know with certain knowledge the truthfulness of what I have brought you of the message, because of the clear signs you have witnessed? The requirement of that knowledge of yours is that you honour and obey me, for whoever knows God and His greatness honours His Messenger, since honouring him is part of honouring God.

Ibn Kathir said: In this there is consolation for the Messenger of God (ﷺ) regarding what he suffered from the disbelievers of his people and others, and a command to him to be patient. Hence he (ﷺ) said: "May God have mercy on Moses! He was harmed with more than this, and he was patient." And in it is a prohibition for the believers against causing him (ﷺ) harm, as God, exalted is He, said:

﴿O you who believe, do not be like those who harmed Moses, but God cleared him of what they said, and he was honoured in the sight of God.﴾ [al-Ahzab: 69] End of quotation.

Abu al-Su'ud said: This is a resumed statement, confirming what precedes it regarding the heinousness of abandoning fighting. "Idh" (when) is in the accusative as an object of an implied verb. The Prophet (ﷺ) was addressed with it by way of tawin (shifting of address). That is: mention to these who turn away from fighting the time when Moses said to the Children of Israel, when he urged them to fight the tyrants, by his saying:

﴿O my people, enter the holy land which God has prescribed for you, and do not turn back on your heels, lest you turn about as losers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 21]. But they did not comply with his command, and disobeyed him in the greatest disobedience, when they said:

﴿O Moses, indeed there are a people of tyrants in it, and we will never enter it until they leave it. If they leave it, then we will enter﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 22], up to his saying:

﴿So go, you and your Lord, and fight; indeed, we are sitting here﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 24]. They persisted in that and harmed him, peace be upon him, with every kind of harm. This is what the eloquence of the noble composition requires, and what sound taste approves. As for what has been said in explaining the causes of the harm, that they harmed him in various ways, by belittling him and disparaging him personally, and by disobeying him in matters whose benefits return to them, and their worship of the calf, and their demand to see God openly, these have no connection to the context. End of summary. Its summary: the context specifies and particularises the type of harm, and the indicator is one of the particularising factors of the general; however, taking it in its general sense is greater in consolation and more fitting, adhering to the generality of the noble wording.

﴿So when they deviated﴾ That is: from the requirement of their knowledge, due to excessive desire and love of the world, ﴿God caused their hearts to deviate﴾ That is: from the path of guidance, and veiled them from the light of perfection, because of turning their choice toward error and misguidance. ﴿And God does not guide the defiantly disobedient people﴾ That is: those who go out of obedience and the way of truth, persisting in deception.

**Commentary on the interpretation of His words, may He be exalted:**

[6] ﴿And when Jesus, son of Mary, said: "O Children of Israel, indeed I am the Messenger of God to you, confirming what came before me of the Torah, and giving good tidings of a Messenger who will come after me, whose name is Ahmad." But when he came to them with clear proofs, they said: "This is manifest magic."﴾

﴿And when Jesus, son of Mary, said: "O Children of Israel, indeed I am the Messenger of God to you, confirming what came before me of the Torah"﴾ That is: which was revealed to Moses, and this is among what calls for belief in him, peace be upon him.

﴿And giving good tidings of a Messenger who will come after me, whose name is Ahmad. But when he came to them with clear proofs﴾ That is: the evidences which God gave him, as proofs of his prophethood. ﴿They said: "This is manifest magic"﴾ That is: evident.

The reference is to what he brought, or to the Prophet ﷺ himself, and calling it magic is hyperbole. The meaning is: my religion is the confirmation of the books of God and His prophets all together, those who came before and those who came after.

**Remarks:**

**First:** Al-Razi and others cited a confirmation of this verse from the Gospel that is present in their hands. It is in the "Gospel of John," in chapter fourteen, as follows:

"If you love me, keep my commandments. And I will pray the Father, and he shall give you another Comforter (Paraclete), that he may abide with you for ever" — as in the printed edition of the years 1821, 1831 and 1833 in the city of London. The word "Paraclete" is Greek, and its original form is Periklutos (Perikletos), meaning "Muhammad" or "Ahmad," as clarified by the author of "Izhar al-Haqq."

The newspaper "al-Mu'ayyad," issue number (3284), page (2), reported under the heading: "Islam Does Not Lack a Fair-Minded Person":

Monsieur Marcais of the School of Oriental Languages said the following:

"Muhammad is the founder of the Islamic religion, and the name Muhammad comes from the root H-M-D. By a strange coincidence (p-5789), the Arab Christians used a name from the same root that is close in meaning to Muhammad, namely Ahmad, to name the Barakilis (Barakilites) with it, and the meaning of Ahmad is 'possessor of praise.' This is what led the scholars of the Islamic religion to establish that the books of the Christians had given good tidings of the coming of the Prophet Muhammad. The Qur'an itself pointed to this in its saying about the Messiah: ﴿And giving good tidings of a Messenger who will come after me, whose name is Ahmad﴾."

Esperanza (Sprenger) said: "This verse points specifically to the phrase in the 'Gospel of John' where the Messiah promised his disciples the sending of one bearing this name." End of quote, verbatim.

As for the "Gospel of Barnabas," it contains explicit, repeated expressions, indeed extensive chapters, in which the name of Muhammad is mentioned explicitly in its narrative, and it says that he is the Messenger of God.

Shaykh Muhammad Bayram transmitted from an English traveler that he saw, in the Papal Library in the Vatican, a copy of the Gospel written in Himyaritic script before the mission of the Prophet ﷺ, in which the Messiah says: ﴿And giving good tidings of a Messenger who will come after me, whose name is Ahmad﴾. This agrees with the text of the noble Qur'an word for word. The monks have replaced the points of "Paraclete" in the recent printings with "the Comforter."

Some of them said: "There is no wonder in these continually renewed distortions with the renewal of editions, for they are the disposition of this people in their sacred books."

*A disposition that is among them, not newly arisen.*

**Third:** The Imam Ibn al-Qayyim said in "Jala' al-Afham": The difference between Muhammad and Ahmad is in two respects:

The first: Muhammad is the one praised with praise after praise, so it indicates the multitude of the praise of those who praise him, and this entails the multitude of the causes of praise in him. "Ahmad" is an elative (af'al al-tafdil) from praise, indicating that the praise he deserves is superior to what others deserve. So "Muhammad" is an increase of praise in quantity, and "Ahmad" is an increase in quality; he is praised with the most praise and the best praise that humanity has offered.

The second respect: Muhammad is the one praised with repeated praise, as previously mentioned, and Ahmad is the one who praises his Lord better than all other praisers. The one name, Muhammad, indicates that he is praised, and the second name, Ahmad, indicates that he is the most praising of those who praise their Lord. This is the analogical reading, for the elative and the exclamative (ta'ajjub), according to the group of Basran grammarians, are only formed from the verb of the doer, not from the verb of the object, on the basis that they are derived only from an intransitive verb, not a transitive one. Others disputed with them and permitted forming them from a verb that falls upon an object, based on the Arabs' saying: "How preoccupied he is with the thing" (ma ash-ghalahu bi-sh-shay').

Then he said: The intended meaning is that he ﷺ was named Muhammad and Ahmad because he is praised more than others are praised and better than others are praised. The two names are then passive (in the sense of the object), and this is the preferred view. This is more eloquent in his praise and more complete in meaning. Had it been intended as the active participle, he would have been named Hammad, one who praises much, just as he was named Muhammad, one who is praised much; for he ﷺ "was the most praising of creation toward his Lord." So if his name were according to the doer, it would have been more fitting for him to be named Hammad, just as the name of his community is "the Hammadun." Also, the two names are derived from his good character and praiseworthy qualities, for which he deserved to be named Muhammad and Ahmad. He is the one whom the people of this world and the Hereafter praise, and whom the people of the heavens and the earth praise. Because of the multitude of his qualities, which exceed counting, he was named with two names from the names of praise, which imply superiority and increase in extent and attribute. End of quote.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted Is He:

[7] ﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah while he is being invited to Islam? And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾

﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah while he is being invited to Islam﴾ means: there is no one more unjust or more aggressive than one who is invited to the apparent Islam, whose reality is clear and which brings him happiness in both abodes, and who then exchanges his response to it for fabricating lies and inventing falsehoods against Allah. This includes his saying of the speech of Allah, Exalted is He, that it is "sorcery," and of His Messenger that he is "a sorcerer." This verse is either a new sentence (mustaʼnafa) establishing the prophethood of the Prophet (ﷺ), serving as a vanguard for the verses that follow, or it completes what precedes it, to condemn what the Israelites (Banu Isra'il) slandered Jesus, peace be upon him, with, while its generality also indicates the censure of everyone who is of their kind. It should not be said that "Islam" supports the first interpretation, because it is the designation of the upright monotheistic creed (al-millah al-hanifiyyah), since it may also be intended in its linguistic meaning. This usage is frequent in many verses. Indeed, the nearer of the two is the first, but the verse's capacity to bear both meanings is among the wonders of the Revelation.

﴿And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ means: those who wronged themselves by their disbelief in what was sent down of the truth.

The discussion on the interpretation of His, the Exalted, saying:

[8] ﴿They want to extinguish the light of Allah with their mouths, but Allah will perfect His light, although the disbelievers dislike it.﴾

﴿They want to extinguish the light of Allah with their mouths, but Allah will perfect His light, although the disbelievers dislike it.﴾ Ibn Jarir said: That is, these speakers say to Muhammad (ﷺ), "This is a sorcerer," wanting to nullify the truth that he brought by their saying that he is a sorcerer and that what he brought is sorcery. But Allah makes the truth manifest, makes His religion prevail, and gives victory to His Messenger over those who oppose him, and that is the perfecting of His light. End of quote.

In ﴿the light of Allah﴾ there is an explicit metaphor (isti'ara tasrihiyya) for His religion, and "extinguishing" (al-itfa') is a supporting metaphor (tarshih). Or the whole construction is a figurative metaphor (isti'ara tamthiliyya), in which their state of striving to nullify the truth is depicted as the state of one who blows on the light of the sun with his mouth to extinguish it, as a mockery and derision of them, just as people say, "He is trying to plaster over the eye of the sun." The second is more eloquent and subtle, and it is the view preferred by al-Zamakhshari.

Regarding the particle lam in ﴿li-yutfi'u﴾ (in order that they extinguish), there are positions of the grammarians (nuhat) established in the extended works, and among the most famous of them is that it is additional (za'ida) to emphasize the meaning of desire, because the lam of causation carries an indication of desire and intention.

(p-5792)

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[9] ﴿It is He who has sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth, to make it prevail over all religion, even though the polytheists dislike it.﴾

﴿It is He who has sent His Messenger﴾ meaning Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿with guidance and the religion of truth, to make it prevail over all religion﴾. Ibn Jarir said: that is, over every religion other than it. And that is at the descent of Jesus, son of Mary, when the community becomes one, and there will be no religion other than Islam.

Al-Zamakhshari said: that is, to make it exalted over all the religions that oppose it. By my life, indeed he has done so, for no religion remains among the religions except that it is overcome and subdued by the religion of Islam. A further verification of a similar verse has already been given at the end of Surah al-Fath, so let it be consulted.

﴿Even though the polytheists dislike it﴾ that is, because of what it contains of pure monotheism and the nullification of polytheism.

Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 61, verses 10–13:

The discussion of the interpretation of His, the Exalted, saying:

[10–13] ﴿O you who have believed, shall I guide you to a transaction that will save you from a painful punishment?﴾ ﴿You believe in Allah and His Messenger and strive in the cause of Allah with your wealth and your lives. That is best for you, if you only knew.﴾ [al-Saff: 11] ﴿He will forgive you your sins and admit you to gardens beneath which rivers flow and pleasant dwellings in gardens of perpetual residence. **Commentary on the interpretation of His words, the Exalted:**

[14] ﴿O you who have believed, be helpers of Allah, as Jesus, son of Mary, said to the disciples, "Who will be my helpers for Allah?" The disciples said, "We are helpers of Allah." So a faction of the Children of Israel believed, and a faction disbelieved. Then We supported those who believed against their enemy, and they became the ones who prevailed.﴾

﴿O you who have believed, be helpers of Allah﴾, meaning: helpers of the truth that He sent down and commanded. ﴿as Jesus, son of Mary, said to the disciples, "Who will be my helpers for Allah?"﴾, meaning: who will be with me and my soldiers, heading toward supporting Allah. ﴿The disciples said, "We are helpers of Allah,"﴾, meaning: we will support His religion and what He commanded, call to it, and sacrifice our lives for it. ﴿So a faction of the Children of Israel believed﴾, meaning: in Jesus, peace be upon him, and they rose up calling to what he was sent with and spreading his call. ﴿and a faction disbelieved﴾ ﴿﴾, meaning: [the believers became] dominant over them through clear proofs, manifest arguments, and overpowering authority. In this there is good news for the believers of divine support for them, as long as they help one another upon the truth, unite upon it, and do not separate from it or forsake it. This is what happened to their predecessors: they agreed and so they ruled, and if they divide, they perish.

(p-٥٧٩٥) **A subtle point:**

The comparison is not to be taken literally, namely the comparison of the believers being helpers of Allah to the statement of Jesus. For there is no basis for comparing a state of being to a statement. Rather, it is to be interpreted by making the comparison in terms of meaning, either by the implied phrase "Say to them, as Jesus said," because it is clear from it and the discourse is directed toward it, or by the implied phrase "Be helpers of Allah, as the disciples were when Jesus said to them: Who will be my helpers for Allah?"

Al-Shihab said: the particle *mā* (ما) here is verbal-masdarian (*maṣdariyyah*, meaning it turns the following clause into a verbal noun), and it together with its clause functions as an adverbial of time. The original sense is: "like the state of the disciples being helpers at the time Jesus spoke." Then the modified element (*al-maẓrūf*) was omitted, and its adverbial was put in its place. The verse has also been considered an instance of *iḥtibāk* (a rhetorical device in which two parallel elements are mentioned so that each omits what is mentioned in the other). The original sense is: "Be helpers of Allah when the Prophet said to you: Who will be my helpers for Allah? As the disciples were helpers of Allah when Jesus said to them: Who will be my helpers for Allah?" So from each of the two parts he omitted what was indicated by the mentioned part in the other. This is a fine statement. End of quotation.
